name: Wen Hair Care

card.summary: Wen by Chaz Dean is a cleansing-conditioner hair-care line that combines washing and conditioning in one product, aimed at softer, smoother-looking hair.
card.note: The FDA investigated consumer reports of hair loss and scalp reactions linked to the product in 2016.

quick.overview:
Wen is a hair-care brand created by stylist Chaz Dean and marketed by Guthy-Renker. Its main product is a cleansing conditioner, a single product meant to replace shampoo and conditioner. Users choose it for softer, smoother-looking hair.

In 2016 the FDA reported 127 consumer complaints of hair loss, breakage, balding, itching and rash, and said it was investigating many more reports made to the companies. The company disputes a link, and dermatologists quoted by NPR named other possible causes.
quick.how: A cleansing conditioner is used in place of shampoo, typically worked through wet hair and rinsed. Users on forums mention it in hair-care routines alongside other products.
quick.risks: The FDA's 2016 alert advised people who have a reaction to stop using the product and see a dermatologist. The FDA did not identify a cause and did not think the product was contaminated.

lead: Wen by Chaz Dean is a hair-care line of cleansing conditioners, products that combine the functions of shampoo and conditioner, created by Chaz Dean and marketed and manufactured by Guthy-Renker.[1]
Users adopt it to wash and condition hair in one step, aiming for softer-looking hair with a simplified routine.

In July 2016 the FDA said it had received 127 reports of hair loss, breakage, balding, itching and rash, more than for any cosmetic hair product, and was reviewing more than 21,000 complaints made to the companies.[1] The company stands behind its products, and dermatologists quoted by NPR listed allergies, stress, pattern baldness and other causes as possible explanations.[1]

chain: Cleansing conditioner replaces shampoo and conditioner
Hair is washed and conditioned in one step
angle.text: People use cleansing conditioners to keep hair looking soft and smooth with a simpler routine, as an alternative to detergent-based shampoo.

paras: As of July 7, 2016 the FDA had received 127 complaints of hair loss, breakage, balding, itching and rash. It had not identified a cause, said it had no reason to think the product was contaminated, and was reviewing quality testing and manufacturing changes.[1] The agency does not approve cosmetics before sale but monitors complaints.[1]

Chaz Dean's representative said the company did not receive 21,000 complaints; the company said it stands behind its products and has cooperated with the FDA. Mediation had begun in late 2015 on a California class-action lawsuit against Guthy-Renker.[1]

Dermatologist Paradi Mirmirani told NPR such reports are very rare; Bruce Brod said allergies to surfactants, preservatives or fragrances are a common cause; Nicole Rogers said pattern baldness and alopecia areata are common causes and she believed the complaints unlikely related to Wen.[1] Brod cautioned about a "herd effect" in online groups.[1]

timeline.event: FDA reports 127 consumer complaints and investigates additional complaints made to the companies.[1]
